Accordingly, future work must investigate the logistics of on-site fabrication including the feasibility of designing and constructing vertical sulfur TES vessels to reduce system footprint and cost. Vertical sulfur TES vessel configuration introduces additional design considerations that require detailed thermo-mechanical investigation, particularly with respect to thermal stress analysis at the vessel floor due to temperature gradients and frictional force interactions between the vessel floor and foundation during transient thermal cyclic operation. Addressing these effects is critical to ensure a fail-safe design and reliable long-term operation. Page 82 of 87 DE-EE0009329 Element 16 Technologies, Inc. Although this project did not complete a CST integrated pilot demonstration, a petroleum refinery customer conducted a successful hazard and operability (HAZOP) and control strategies review for a scaled-up 250-ton molten sulfur TES system integrated with their on-site solar thermal facility. This independent review provides confidence in the feasibility of integrating sulfur TES with commercial CST systems at industrial scale. In addition, Element 16 is working on a California Energy Commission funded project focused on integrating a pilot sulfur TES unit with an operational mining facility in California. This project will provide valuable experience in system integration, permitting, and safety validation under real-world industrial conditions. Future development efforts will focus on implementing advanced control strategies, such as model predictive control, that incorporate system state feedback and predictive forecasts to enable reliable operation of sulfur TES integrated with dynamically varying solar thermal outputs while meeting industrial process heat requirements. Element 16 is also pursuing the integration of sulfur TES tied to the electric grid, which is increasingly decarbonized with renewable generation. The testing of the pilot sulfur TES unit with an electric heater conducted in this project directly informs the design and operation of such grid-tied systems. Integration of sulfur thermal storage can significantly improve the economics of grid-tied electrotechnology for industrial process heat by storing energy during periods of low electricity prices and delivering the stored heat when electricity prices are high. This approach aligns with the broader goals of improving energy efficiency and accelerating industrial decarbonization. Element 16 has validated the market potential for this model in European countries such as Finland, where regulatory frameworks allow thermal energy storage systems to access wholesale electricity markets for time-of-use heat arbitrage. Building strong partnerships with key stakeholders in the renewable energy sector and collaborating on joint research initiatives like this one will be crucial to those efforts. Element 16 will also continue to engage with customers to provide tailored solutions and comprehensive support for their unique energy requirements. Element 16 has begun early commercialization steps, including its first unsubsidized purchase orders for front-end engineering design (FEED) and detailed engineering of a sulfur TES pilot with a solar steam field. In parallel, the team is executing a CEC-funded pilot-scale sulfur TES unit at Searles Valley Minerals’ Mojave Desert facility, directly supporting their Zero Net Energy and industrial decarbonization goals.
